«The Scapegoat» — William Holman Hunt  
💰 $145,000  

Hunt traveled to the Dead Sea, enduring extreme heat and harsh conditions to paint this scene firsthand. For the Pre-Raphaelites, truth required direct experience — no studio could replicate such reality.  

The painting shows a lone goat in a barren, salt-scarred wasteland, surrounded by animal bones. Inspired by the Yom Kippur ritual, it depicts the goat bearing the people’s sins, exiled into desolation. This image of profound isolation captures both physical and spiritual abandonment.  

Contemporaries were baffled — expecting dramatic biblical figures, they found instead an almost empty landscape. Yet this boldness made it one of Hunt’s most celebrated works and a lasting symbol of Pre-Raphaelite ideals.

All of this makes copper one of the defining materials of the next decade — alongside uranium and rare earth metals.

📌 Browser Extensions: Why a Chrome Wallet Is Its Own Risk Layer

Main Points
⏺ A browser wallet lives in the same environment as sites, scripts, and other extensions
⏺ Browser or website attacks can push users into dangerous signatures
⏺ This post explains why wallet convenience needs discipline

1️⃣ Core Idea — extensions make dApp access easy, but they place your wallet inside the browser flow.
2️⃣ Attack Surface — phishing sites, fake popups, malicious extensions, and swapped links.
3️⃣ Common Mistake — users recognize the interface and sign without reading the action.
4️⃣ Separation — use a dedicated browser/profile for crypto instead of mixing it with daily browsing.
5️⃣ Practical Hygiene — keep extensions minimal, use bookmarks, verify domains, and simulate large transactions.

Final Thoughts

Browser wallets are convenient, but they live in a noisy environment. The more clutter around them, the higher the chance of signing the wrong thing.

What does “gas” mean in crypto? 

“Gas” is important in the world of crypto. Simply put, gas is the payment needed when making a transaction or interacting with a smart contract on a blockchain — i.e., the network fee you pay. 

Gas is usually paid in the given blockchain’s native cryptocurrency — e.g., ETH is used for transactions on Ethereum, and BNB is used for the same on BNB Smart Chain). These fees go to miners or validators responsible for keeping networks secure and confirming transactions. Gas fees also prevent spam on the network, keeping the blockchain running smoothly.

Let's talk about that brand-new pool you just saw launch. How does it earn anything on day one? The answer is simple: Arbitrage.

The moment a pool goes live, its price can slightly differ from the prices on major centralized exchanges (CEX). Smart traders and automated bots, known as arbitrageurs, are constantly scanning for these tiny gaps. They buy where it’s cheap and sell where it’s dear.

This isn't theoretical volume. Even today, with only a handful of live pools on Gala Swap, millions of dollars in arbitrage volume are flowing through the platform daily. Every single one of those trades pays a fee to the liquidity provider (LP).

Real Volume, Real Fees (Not "Farm Token" Emissions)

This is what makes Gala Swap different. The yield isn't based on inflationary "farm token" emissions that you have to constantly race against.

The LP rewards on Gala Swap are generated by real trading activity—the essential work of keeping the DEX price in sync with the broader market. When you provide liquidity, you become the infrastructure that makes this flow possible, and you earn your share of the fees from that volume.

The Real Gold Rush: Expanding the Surface

The current volume is impressive, but here’s what’s truly exciting: the bottleneck isn't the demand from traders; it's the surface area available for the arbitrage engine to work across.

A few dozen pools can only capture a few dozen tokens' worth of flow. Imagine this same efficient arbitrage engine running across hundreds of pools that simply don't exist yet.

The Takeaway:

The traders are ready. The volume is real. The arbitrage engine is already running. What's missing is the liquidity to serve that volume and capture those fees across a much broader range of pairs.

Hormuz: Two Powers, One Tollbooth

On Friday, August 14, Donald Trump told a law-enforcement audience on Long Island that, “after we finish defeating Iran,” he would “pretty soon” declare the Strait of Hormuz “a territory of the United States.” He laughed as he said it. Then he supplied the logic: “We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.” 

This was not a legal claim. It was a victory-lap fantasy built on a real instrument of coercion. The United States restored its naval blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 after the U.S.-Iran ceasefire memorandum collapsed. Iran had also restricted traffic through Hormuz. The strait is not paralyzed by slogans alone. It is squeezed from both shores by competing armed permissions. 

Trump previously floated a 20% “reimbursement fee” on cargo passing through the strait, before replacing it with promised Gulf trade and investment deals. 

Iran, meanwhile, has sought recognition of its own control over passage and proposed payments for what it calls security and navigation services. 

International-law experts cited by NPR said such fees would violate the rules governing passage through an international strait. 

So the dispute is not really about sovereignty. It is about who gets to sell the escort, write the rules and collect the tariff.

While the speeches were still making the rounds, the UAE said Iran had carried out a hostile missile attack on two vessels linked to Abu Dhabi National Oil Company as they transited Hormuz. No crew members were injured. 

The UAE Foreign Ministry called the attack a violation of freedom of navigation and accused the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of using the strait for “economic coercion or blackmail.” 

The attack’s technical details remain contested. Iranian sources have claimed underwater drones were used. Reuters-verified satellite imagery showed oil slicks near Iran’s Qeshm and Sirri islands, evidence that the contest for maritime control is already leaving damage on the water. 

Trump can promise a new American territory. Tehran can promise that Hormuz will remain Iranian.

The actual authority is exercised by whoever can stop the next tanker.

📣 EU to revise MiCA rules in 2027 amid US stablecoin push 

⚠️ European Union officials are preparing to revise the bloc’s MiCA crypto framework in 2027 as foreign stablecoin restrictions and faster U.S. rulemaking expose gaps in the existing regime. The planned revision would examine how MiCA treats stablecoins issued outside the European Union. Current requirements have prevented several foreign issuers from receiving authorization, limiting their access to regulated exchanges across the bloc.

💬 “Reopening the file seems unavoidable at this stage,” an unidentified European diplomat told Euronews.

🔗 The diplomat cited positions taken by European institutions, including the European Central Bank, along with changes in global regulation and digital-asset technology. No final proposal has been published. Any amendment would need to pass through the EU’s legislative process before taking effect. The consultation covers developments that have occurred since MiCA entered into application. Its deadline has been extended to Sept. 30, with crypto issuers, service providers, regulators, central banks and finance ministries invited to respond.
